hook.text: What's 2 + 2? Instant. What's 17 × 24? You need to slow down and work it out. Two different systems.

buildup.text: Kahneman calls them System 1 and System 2. Fast and intuitive versus slow and deliberate.

discovery.text: System 1 runs automatically—pattern matching, gut feelings, snap judgments. It handles 95% of decisions.

twist.text: System 2 feels like 'you' thinking. But it's lazy. It often just rubber-stamps whatever System 1 suggests.

climax.text: Most errors come from System 1 answering a hard question with an easier one—and you never noticing.

punchline.text: You have two minds. The fast one usually wins.

quiz.question: Which system handles most of our daily decisions?

hook.text: Classical economics assumed humans weigh all options and pick the best. Herbert Simon said: that's impossible.

buildup.text: We lack the time, information, and brainpower to compute optimal choices. Our rationality is bounded.

discovery.text: Instead, we 'satisfice'—search until we find an option that's good enough, then stop looking.

twist.text: Satisficing often beats optimizing. Maximizers search longer, choose slower, and feel less satisfied.

climax.text: Simon won the Nobel Prize for showing that good-enough decisions usually outperform perfect ones.

punchline.text: Good enough is often better than best.

quiz.question: What is 'satisficing'?

hook.text: A grocery store offered 24 jams for tasting. Shoppers loved the variety—but almost nobody bought one.

buildup.text: When the display shrank to 6 jams, sales increased tenfold. Fewer options, more decisions.

discovery.text: Barry Schwartz called this the paradox of choice: more options create more anxiety and less satisfaction.

twist.text: With many choices, every option carries an opportunity cost. You imagine the roads not taken.

climax.text: Choice overload paralyzes the decision system. When everything is available, nothing feels right.

punchline.text: More options, less happiness.

quiz.question: What happened when the jam display shrank from 24 to 6?

hook.text: Israeli judges granted parole 65% of the time in the morning but nearly 0% right before lunch.

buildup.text: The decisions hadn't changed—the judges had. Their ability to decide well had drained over time.

discovery.text: Decision fatigue is real: each choice depletes a shared mental resource, making the next one worse.

twist.text: When depleted, people either choose the default option or avoid deciding at all.

climax.text: This is why Steve Jobs wore the same outfit daily. Eliminating trivial decisions preserves the resource.

punchline.text: Decisions are a budget. Spend them wisely.

quiz.question: What happens to decision quality over a long session?

hook.text: In Libet's experiment, the brain showed readiness to act 350 milliseconds before the person 'decided' to move.

buildup.text: The conscious feeling of deciding came after the brain had already committed. Decision preceded awareness.

discovery.text: Dijksterhuis found that for complex choices—like picking a car—unconscious thought outperforms analysis.

twist.text: But for simple choices with few variables, conscious deliberation is better. Complexity determines the tool.

climax.text: Much of what you call intuition is your brain running a massive parallel process you can't observe.

punchline.text: Sometimes the best decision is the one you didn't think about.

quiz.question: What did Libet's experiment reveal?
options: The brain is too slow for decisions

hook.text: After a plane crash makes headlines, ticket sales drop—even though flying just got statistically no less safe.

buildup.text: We judge frequency by how easily examples come to mind. Vivid events feel common; quiet ones feel rare.

discovery.text: Tversky and Kahneman named this the availability heuristic: ease of recall replaces actual probability.

twist.text: Shark attacks feel more likely than falling coconuts. Reality: coconuts kill more people every year.

climax.text: Media amplifies this bias. Whatever is covered most feels most dangerous, regardless of real data.

punchline.text: If you can picture it, you overestimate it.

quiz.question: What does the availability heuristic use to judge frequency?

hook.text: Spin a rigged wheel showing 10 or 65. Then ask: what percentage of African countries are in the UN? Answers follow the wheel.

buildup.text: People who saw 10 guessed around 25%. Those who saw 65 guessed around 45%. A random number moved their estimate.

discovery.text: This is anchoring: the first number you encounter pulls your judgment toward it, even when irrelevant.

twist.text: Experts are anchored too. Experienced judges give harsher sentences after rolling higher dice.

climax.text: Retailers exploit anchoring constantly. The 'original price' sticker exists only to make the sale price feel good.

punchline.text: The first number wins—even when it's nonsense.

quiz.question: What is anchoring?
options: A first number biasing subsequent estimates

hook.text: Linda is 31, outspoken, and studied philosophy. Is she more likely a bank teller—or a feminist bank teller?

buildup.text: Most people say feminist bank teller. But that's logically impossible—it's a subset of all bank tellers.

discovery.text: We judge probability by resemblance. Linda 'looks like' a feminist, so we ignore base rates entirely.

twist.text: Even statisticians fall for this. Narrative fit overrides mathematical logic in the human mind.

climax.text: Tversky and Kahneman showed that we confuse 'sounds right' with 'is probable' across countless domains.

punchline.text: A good story beats good math—in your brain.

quiz.question: What is the conjunction fallacy?
options: Judging a specific combo as more likely than its parts

hook.text: Which city has more people: San Diego or San Antonio? If you've heard of one and not the other, pick the familiar one.

buildup.text: Goldstein and Gigerenzer found that recognition alone is a powerful decision tool in many domains.

discovery.text: German students outperformed Americans on U.S. city population rankings—because they only recognized the big ones.

twist.text: More information can actually hurt. Americans knew too many cities and second-guessed themselves.

climax.text: Sometimes ignorance is a feature. Knowing less forces you to rely on a simple, often accurate, cue.

punchline.text: Sometimes knowing less helps you choose better.

quiz.question: Why did German students outperform Americans on U.S. city rankings?
options: They only recognized the biggest cities

hook.text: A doctor in the ER has seconds to decide: is this chest pain a heart attack? They don't run a full analysis.

buildup.text: Gerd Gigerenzer showed that simple decision trees—check one cue, then decide—often beat complex models.

discovery.text: These are fast-and-frugal heuristics: rules that use minimal information and still get it right most of the time.

twist.text: In unpredictable environments, simple rules outperform algorithms because they don't overfit noisy data.

climax.text: Evolution designed our brains for good-enough speed, not perfect accuracy. And it works.

punchline.text: Simple rules often beat complex models.

quiz.question: When do fast-and-frugal heuristics perform best?

hook.text: A patient with frontal lobe damage had a perfect IQ but couldn't choose a restaurant or schedule a meeting.

buildup.text: Antonio Damasio studied Elliot, who could analyze options endlessly but never commit to a choice.

discovery.text: Damasio proposed that emotions mark options with gut feelings—somatic markers—that guide decisions.

twist.text: Without these emotional markers, pure reason is paralyzed. Logic alone can't break a tie.

climax.text: Emotions aren't the enemy of good decisions. They're a required ingredient. Strip them and you're stuck.

punchline.text: Without emotion, reason can't choose.

quiz.question: What are somatic markers?
options: Emotional gut feelings that guide choices

hook.text: Four decks of cards. Two give big wins but bigger losses. Two give small wins but steady gains. Choose.

buildup.text: Healthy players start shifting to the safe decks after about 50 cards—before they can explain why.

discovery.text: Their skin conductance spikes before reaching for a bad deck. The body knows before the mind does.

twist.text: Patients with prefrontal damage never shift. They keep picking the risky decks, losing everything.

climax.text: The Iowa Gambling Task proved that emotion-based learning is essential for adaptive decision-making.

punchline.text: Your body learns the odds before your mind does.

quiz.question: What did healthy players' skin conductance show?
options: It spiked before choosing bad decks

hook.text: After the 9/11 attacks, 1,500 extra Americans died in car accidents—they avoided flying out of fear.

buildup.text: Fear distorts risk assessment. It makes rare dangers feel imminent and safe choices feel reckless.

discovery.text: The amygdala hijacks decision-making during fear, bypassing slower, rational evaluation systems.

twist.text: This was adaptive for predators on the savanna. For modern risks involving statistics, it backfires.

climax.text: Fear doesn't just color one decision—it shifts your entire risk threshold, making you cautious about everything.

punchline.text: Fear doesn't calculate—it vetoes.

quiz.question: What happened to U.S. car deaths after 9/11?
options: They increased as people avoided flying

hook.text: You miss a flight by 5 minutes and feel devastated. Miss it by 2 hours and you shrug. Same outcome, different pain.

buildup.text: Regret scales with how close you came to a better outcome. Near-misses sting more than distant ones.

discovery.text: We also feel more regret for actions than inactions—even when doing nothing costs more.

twist.text: Anticipated regret shapes future decisions. People avoid choices that might later make them feel bad.

climax.text: This drives loss aversion: the pain of losing feels twice as strong as the pleasure of winning the same amount.

punchline.text: We decide not just for outcomes—but to avoid future regret.

quiz.question: Why does missing a flight by 5 minutes hurt more than by 2 hours?

hook.text: You swear you'll eat healthy—then see a chocolate cake. In a cold state, you made a hot-state decision.

buildup.text: Loewenstein showed that we systematically fail to predict how emotions will change our future choices.

discovery.text: In a cold (calm) state, you underestimate how hunger, anger, or desire will hijack your plans.

twist.text: In a hot (emotional) state, you can't imagine ever feeling calm again. Each state is blind to the other.

climax.text: This 'empathy gap' explains relapse, impulse buying, and why New Year's resolutions fail by February.

punchline.text: Calm you and emotional you are almost different people.

quiz.question: What is the 'empathy gap' in decision making?
options: Inability to predict how emotions change choices

hook.text: Would you prefer a sure $500 or a 50% chance of $1,000? Most people take the sure thing. Now flip it to losses.

buildup.text: For losses, people gamble: they'd rather risk losing $1,000 than accept a sure $500 loss.

discovery.text: Kahneman and Tversky's prospect theory: we're risk-averse for gains but risk-seeking for losses.

twist.text: The value function is asymmetric. Losing $100 hurts roughly twice as much as gaining $100 feels good.

climax.text: This won Kahneman the Nobel Prize and revolutionized economics. People aren't rational—they're loss-averse.

punchline.text: Losses loom larger than gains—always.

quiz.question: How does prospect theory describe our response to losses?
options: We become risk-seeking to avoid losses

hook.text: A surgery has a 90% survival rate. The same surgery has a 10% mortality rate. Which sounds better?

buildup.text: Same numbers, different frames. Yet people overwhelmingly prefer the 'survival' frame and reject 'mortality.'

discovery.text: The framing effect: how information is presented changes the decision, even when the facts are identical.

twist.text: Doctors are susceptible too. Framing a treatment as '200 saved out of 600' versus '400 die' shifts their recommendations.

climax.text: Politicians, advertisers, and negotiators all exploit framing. The fact is the same—the lens changes everything.

punchline.text: Same fact, different frame, different choice.

quiz.question: What does the framing effect demonstrate?
options: Presentation changes decisions even with identical facts

hook.text: You've watched 90 minutes of a terrible film. You stay because you've 'already invested the time.'

buildup.text: The sunk cost fallacy: past investments—time, money, effort—shouldn't affect future decisions, but they do.

discovery.text: Rationally, only future costs and benefits matter. The money already spent is gone regardless.

twist.text: Businesses sink billions into failing projects because leaders won't abandon their prior commitments.

climax.text: The Concorde jet was continued for decades despite guaranteed losses—now economists call it the Concorde fallacy.

punchline.text: What you've spent shouldn't decide what you do next.

quiz.question: What is the sunk cost fallacy?
options: Letting past investment drive future decisions

hook.text: Urn A has 50 red and 50 black balls. Urn B has 100 balls, unknown mix. Most people choose Urn A. Why?

buildup.text: Daniel Ellsberg showed that people prefer known probabilities over unknown ones—even when the math is identical.

discovery.text: This is ambiguity aversion: uncertainty about the odds feels worse than the odds themselves.

twist.text: In real life, most risks involve ambiguity, not clean probabilities. We rarely know the true odds.

climax.text: Ambiguity aversion explains why people avoid new investments, unfamiliar foods, and unknown paths—even promising ones.

punchline.text: We fear not knowing the odds more than bad odds.

quiz.question: What is ambiguity aversion?
options: Preferring known odds over unknown ones

hook.text: Ask people: are you an above-average driver? About 80% say yes. Mathematically, they can't all be right.

buildup.text: Overconfidence is one of the most reliable findings in judgment research. It appears in every culture and profession.

discovery.text: It comes in three forms: overestimating your ability, your knowledge, and your precision of forecasts.

twist.text: Experts are often more overconfident than novices. Greater knowledge inflates certainty faster than accuracy.

climax.text: A calibration study found that when doctors were 90% sure of a diagnosis, they were right only 50% of the time.

punchline.text: Confidence grows faster than competence.

quiz.question: What is the overconfidence effect?

hook.text: In Asch's experiment, people picked an obviously wrong answer just because everyone else in the room did.

buildup.text: 75% of participants conformed at least once. They could see the right answer—but chose the group's answer.

discovery.text: Brain scans show conformity actually changes perception. The visual cortex shifts—you don't just say the wrong answer, you see it.

twist.text: Even one dissenter breaks the spell. If a single person gives the right answer, conformity drops to 5%.

climax.text: We're wired to align with the group because ancestral survival depended on tribal acceptance.

punchline.text: One dissenting voice can free an entire room.

quiz.question: What dramatically reduced conformity in Asch's experiment?
options: One dissenter giving the right answer

hook.text: Kitty Genovese was attacked while 38 neighbors allegedly watched. None called for help.

buildup.text: Darley and Latané found that the more people present, the less likely any individual is to intervene.

discovery.text: It's diffusion of responsibility: everyone assumes someone else will act. So nobody does.

twist.text: Alone with a victim, 85% help. In a group of five, only 31% do. The crowd doesn't help—it paralyzes.

climax.text: Knowing the effect helps. People trained about the bystander effect are significantly more likely to act.

punchline.text: In a crowd, nobody's job becomes everybody's excuse.

quiz.question: What causes the bystander effect?

hook.text: I offer to split $10. I keep $9, you get $1. Take it or we both get nothing. Most people reject the deal.

buildup.text: Rationally you should accept any amount over zero. A dollar is better than nothing. But fairness overrides logic.

discovery.text: The ultimatum game reveals that humans will pay a cost to punish unfairness—even when it hurts them.

twist.text: Brain scans show the anterior insula lights up on unfair offers—the same region activated by disgust.

climax.text: Cross-cultural studies show variation, but every society rejects extremely unfair splits. Fairness is universal.

punchline.text: We'd rather have nothing than accept injustice.

quiz.question: What do most people do with a very unfair offer in the ultimatum game?
options: Reject it, even at personal cost

hook.text: The Bay of Pigs invasion was approved by brilliant advisors who privately had doubts—but said nothing.

buildup.text: Irving Janis coined 'groupthink': when cohesive groups prioritize harmony over honest evaluation.

discovery.text: Symptoms include illusion of invulnerability, self-censorship, and pressure on dissenters to conform.

twist.text: The group doesn't suppress dissent on purpose. Members genuinely believe the group can't be wrong.

climax.text: NASA's Challenger disaster is another case: engineers warned about O-ring failure, but group pressure silenced them.

punchline.text: The smarter the group, the more dangerous its silence.

quiz.question: What is groupthink?
options: Groups prioritizing harmony over critical thinking
Thinking as an individual in a group

hook.text: Countries that make organ donation opt-out instead of opt-in see donation rates jump from 15% to over 90%.

buildup.text: Thaler and Sunstein call this a 'nudge': redesigning the choice environment without removing any options.

discovery.text: Defaults are enormously powerful because people tend to stick with whatever is pre-selected.

twist.text: Nudges are controversial. Critics call it paternalism—manipulating choices while pretending people are free.

climax.text: The UK created a 'Nudge Unit' inside government. Its interventions have saved billions in tax collection alone.

punchline.text: Change the default, change the decision.

quiz.question: What is a 'nudge' in decision science?
options: Redesigning choice environments without removing options

hook.text: When hospitals introduced a simple surgery checklist, complications dropped 36% and deaths dropped 47%.

buildup.text: Atul Gawande showed that experts fail not from ignorance but from forgetting steps under pressure.

discovery.text: Checklists work by offloading memory demands. They free up cognitive resources for judgment and adaptation.

twist.text: Pilots adopted checklists after a deadly crash in 1935. Before that, flying was considered 'too complex to list.'

climax.text: The key insight: good decisions aren't about being smarter. They're about building systems that catch errors.

punchline.text: The checklist doesn't replace expertise—it protects it.

quiz.question: Why do checklists improve expert performance?
options: They prevent forgetting steps under pressure

hook.text: Before starting a project, imagine it has failed spectacularly. Now explain why. This is a premortem.

buildup.text: Gary Klein invented the technique: projecting failure makes hidden risks visible before they strike.

discovery.text: It works because it gives people permission to voice doubts. In a regular meeting, dissent feels risky.

twist.text: Groups running premortems identify 30% more risks than groups using standard planning methods.

climax.text: The premortem flips optimism bias on its head. Instead of asking 'how will we succeed,' you ask 'how did we fail.'

punchline.text: Imagining failure is the best way to prevent it.

quiz.question: What is a premortem?
options: Imagining a project has failed and analyzing why
An autopsy of a past failure

hook.text: A test is 99% accurate. You test positive. What's the chance you're actually sick? Most people say 99%. They're wrong.

buildup.text: If the disease affects 1 in 10,000, most positives are false. The base rate—how common the condition is—matters enormously.

discovery.text: Base rate neglect is our tendency to ignore background frequencies and focus only on the specific case.

twist.text: Even doctors fall for it. In one study, 45% of physicians got the base rate problem wrong.

climax.text: Thinking in natural frequencies—'1 in 10,000 people'—instead of percentages dramatically improves accuracy.

punchline.text: Always ask: how common is this in the first place?

quiz.question: What is base rate neglect?

hook.text: At a county fair in 1906, 800 people guessed the weight of an ox. The average guess was off by one pound.

buildup.text: Francis Galton was stunned. No individual was accurate, but the crowd's average was nearly perfect.

discovery.text: Crowd wisdom works when opinions are diverse, independent, and aggregated. Individual errors cancel out.

twist.text: But if people see each other's guesses, independence breaks. Social influence destroys crowd wisdom.

climax.text: Prediction markets work on this principle: aggregate independent bets and you get remarkably accurate forecasts.

punchline.text: A crowd of independent thinkers beats any single expert.

quiz.question: What condition is essential for crowd wisdom to work?

hook.text: You believe there's a 30% chance it'll rain. Then you see dark clouds. How should your estimate change?

buildup.text: Bayes' theorem gives the exact answer: update your prior belief with new evidence to get a better estimate.

discovery.text: Good forecasters think this way: start with a base rate, then nudge it with each new piece of information.

twist.text: Most people overreact to dramatic evidence and underreact to quiet statistical evidence. We're bad Bayesians.

climax.text: Philip Tetlock found that 'superforecasters' beat intelligence agencies by consistently applying Bayesian updates.

punchline.text: Update in small steps. Never be 100% sure of anything.

quiz.question: What does Bayesian thinking require?
